cues.text: A scalar is described by a numerical magnitude with its relevant unit, while a
vector also carries direction.
Mass and elapsed time are scalar examples.
Displacement and force are vector examples.
A vector is often drawn as an arrow whose length represents magnitude and
whose
orientation represents direction.
In this algebra class we use free vectors, so translating an arrow without
rotating or changing its length preserves the vector.
Equal free vectors have identical components in the same coordinate system.
Opposite vectors have equal magnitude and reversed direction; adding one to
its
opposite gives the zero vector.
The zero vector has magnitude zero and every component zero, but no unique
direction or associated unit direction.
Equal magnitudes alone do not make two vectors equal: eastward and northward
displacements of the same length are different vectors.
A position vector depends on the chosen origin, while a displacement between
two fixed points is their difference.
Keep the distinction between a vector and its nonnegative magnitude in
notation
and in calculations.
A signed component can be negative without making the vector's magnitude
negative.
An orthonormal Cartesian basis has three mutually perpendicular unit vectors,
conventionally called i, j and k.
A space vector is written as its x component times i plus its y component
times
j plus its z component times k.
A vector in the x y plane has z component zero and can be recorded using only
its first two components.
Its magnitude follows from the Pythagorean theorem: square the components, add
and take the nonnegative root.
The vector three, four, zero has length five, while two, negative one, two has
length three.
Components are signed scalar coefficients, so a negative y coefficient points
opposite to the positive y basis direction.
The magnitude formula assumes perpendicular unit axes; it cannot be copied
unchanged to an arbitrary nonorthogonal basis.
Vectors are equal precisely when corresponding components in the same basis
are
equal.
Write a zero component explicitly when it helps avoid confusing a plane vector
with a different space vector.
A point's coordinate triple and a vector's component triple may use the same
numbers, but their geometric roles should still be identified.
Vector addition describes a combined displacement.
In the triangle construction, translate the second vector so its tail starts
at
the head of the first; the resultant runs from the first tail to the final
head.
In the parallelogram construction, place both tails together and use the
diagonal from that common tail.
These two constructions give the same vector.
Algebraically, add corresponding components.
For u equal to three, zero, zero and v equal to zero, four, zero, the sum is
three, four, zero, whose magnitude is five.
Adding the two magnitudes would instead give seven, which is not the resultant
length because the directions differ.
Vector addition is commutative and associative, so the order and grouping of a
sum do not change its result.
The zero vector is its identity.
For a closed polygon of successive displacements returning to its start, the
vector sum is zero even though the total distance travelled can be positive.
The resultant magnitude lies between the absolute difference and the sum of
the
two input magnitudes.
The endpoint cases correspond to collinear directions.
Subtraction means adding the opposite vector.
If u is two, negative one, three and v is negative one, four, one, their sum
is
one, three, four.
Their difference u minus v is three, negative five, two.
Each subtraction acts on the entire corresponding component, so subtracting
negative one adds one.
Reversing the order gives v minus u equal to negative three, five, negative
two, the opposite of the first difference.
Subtraction is therefore not commutative.
If u and v are drawn from a common tail, u minus v points from the head of v
to
the head of u.
This picture helps verify the order of a displacement calculation.
The magnitude of a difference is unchanged when its sign is reversed, even
though the vector itself changes direction.
The identity u minus u equal to the zero vector holds component by component.
Keep brackets around a vector being subtracted or multiplied by a negative
scalar so every component receives the sign.
A component check is often the quickest way to catch an arrow drawn in the
wrong direction.
Multiplying a vector by a real scalar multiplies each component by that
scalar.
Its magnitude is multiplied by the absolute value of the scalar.
A positive scalar preserves direction, a negative scalar reverses it, and zero
gives the zero vector.
For u equal to two, negative one, two, the length is three.
Multiplication by negative two gives negative four, two, negative four, with
magnitude six.
To construct the unit vector in the direction of a nonzero u, divide the
vector
by its positive magnitude.
Here the answer is two thirds, negative one third, two thirds.
Its squared component sum is one and it has the same orientation as u.
The opposite unit vector is its negative.
A requested vector of length L in the direction of u is L times this unit
vector, for nonnegative L.
Normalizing the zero vector is undefined because its length is zero and it has
no unique direction.
Scalar multiplication distributes over vector sums, and vector addition
distributes over sums of scalar coefficients.
These laws make component calculations consistent with the geometric scaling
of arrows.
With a chosen origin, let a and b be the position vectors of points A and B.
The displacement from A to B is b minus a, not their sum.
For A at one, negative one, two and B at four, five, negative one, the
displacement is three, six, negative three.
Changing the origin changes both position vectors by the same translation, so
their difference remains unchanged.
Position vectors also express the internal section formula.
If A P to P B is m to n with positive m and n, the position of P is n a
plus m b divided by m plus n.
For ratio one to two, this gives two a plus b divided by three, or P at two,
one, one in this example.
The displacement A P is one third of A B, so its length is half of P B as
required.
Equal weights give the midpoint, five halves, two, one half.
The same vector reasoning works in two and three dimensions.
Verify the ratio and collinearity together; a point with a matching distance
ratio alone need not lie on the endpoint line.
A linear combination scales vectors and adds the results.
To express w equal to three, two as alpha times u equal to one, zero plus beta
times v equal to one, one, compare components.
The y equation gives beta equal to two, and the x equation then gives alpha
equal to one.
Since these two input vectors are nonparallel, the representation of every
plane vector in their span is unique.
If the input vectors are parallel, there may be no representation of a
particular target or multiple representations, so do not assume uniqueness
without checking directions.
Two nonzero vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other.
Thus two, negative one, two and negative four, two, negative four are parallel
with opposite orientation.
Collinearity of points A, B and C is tested using the displacements A B and A
C, rather than their position vectors alone.
The zero vector is algebraically a multiple of every vector but has no unique
direction.
Handle that case explicitly when a question speaks about an angle or a
parallel
direction.
The scalar product, or dot product, multiplies corresponding components and
adds them to give a scalar.
For nonzero vectors it also equals the product of their magnitudes times
cosine
of their angle, where the vector angle ranges from zero to pi.
The vectors one, one, zero and one, negative one, zero have dot product zero
and are perpendicular.
For one, zero, zero and negative one, one, zero, the dot product is negative
one and the product of lengths is square root of two.
Their cosine is negative one over square root of two, giving angle three pi
over four.
Keep the sign when finding a vector angle.
Taking an absolute value would instead give the smaller angle between the
unoriented supporting lines, a different question.
A positive dot product indicates an acute vector angle, a negative one an
obtuse angle and zero a right angle, provided both vectors are nonzero.
The dot product with the zero vector is zero but no vector angle with it is
defined.
Before using the angle formula, check both magnitudes are positive and the
normalized result lies between negative one and one.
The dot product is commutative and distributes over addition.
In particular, u dotted with itself equals its squared magnitude.
Expanding the dot product of u plus v with itself gives the squared resultant
length as magnitude u squared plus magnitude v squared plus twice u dot v.
The difference formula has a minus sign before that last term.
If the magnitudes are three and four and the vector angle is pi over three,
the
dot product is six.
The sum has squared length thirty seven, while the difference has squared
length thirteen.
Their squared lengths add to fifty, twice the sum of nine and sixteen,
illustrating the parallelogram law.
Another expansion gives u plus v dotted with u minus v equal to magnitude u
squared minus magnitude v squared because the mixed terms cancel.
Equal length input vectors therefore produce perpendicular sum and difference
when those two resulting vectors are both nonzero.
If either result is zero, the dot identity still holds but a right angle is
not
defined.
Expand first and then apply the relevant angle or magnitude condition, rather
than treating dot products as ordinary products of lengths in every situation.
Projection separates the part of a vector along a chosen nonzero direction
from
the perpendicular remainder.
The signed scalar projection of u on v is u dot v divided by magnitude v.
The vector projection is u dot v divided by magnitude v squared, multiplied by
v.
For u equal to three, four, zero and v equal to one, zero, zero, the scalar
projection is three and the projected vector is three, zero, zero.
The remaining vector zero, four, zero is perpendicular to v.
Reversing v reverses the sign of the scalar projection because the oriented
measuring direction changes.
The vector projection onto the same axis is unchanged because both its
coefficient and the direction vector reverse.
Thus a scalar projection, a projection length and a projected vector are
related but different objects.
The nonnegative projection length is the absolute value of the signed scalar
projection.
Projection onto the zero vector is undefined.
Check a computed vector projection by verifying that it is parallel to v and
that subtracting it from u leaves a vector with zero dot product with v.
The vector product, or cross product, of two space vectors is another vector
perpendicular to both.
Its direction follows the right hand rule in a right handed coordinate basis.
The cyclic basis products i cross j equal k, j cross k equal i, and k
cross i equal j are positive; reversing any order gives the negative.
In components, the x component is u y times v z minus u z times v y.
The y component is u z times v x minus u x times v z.
The z component is u x times v y minus u y times v x.
For u equal to one, two, three and v equal to two, negative one, one, these
give five, five, negative five.
Dotting the result with either original vector gives zero, checking
perpendicularity.
That check alone does not distinguish a vector from its negative, so also
verify the chosen order and right hand sign.
Unlike a dot product, a cross product has vector components rather than a
single scalar value.
Plane vectors can be embedded in three dimensions by adding zero z components
before taking their cross product.
The magnitude of the cross product equals the product of the input magnitudes
times sine of their angle.
Geometrically, this is the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors
as adjacent sides.
Half that magnitude is the corresponding triangle area.
For three, zero, zero and zero, four, zero, the cross product is zero, zero,
twelve, so the parallelogram area is twelve and the triangle area is six.
A triangle from points A, B and C uses the two side displacements B minus A
and
C minus A, both starting at the same vertex.
For A at one, zero, zero, B at three, zero, zero and C at one, three, zero,
these side lengths are two and three at a right angle, giving triangle area
three.
A zero cross product for two nonzero vectors means the directions are parallel
or opposite.
If an input is zero, the product is also zero but its direction and angle need
separate interpretation.
Cross products distribute over vector sums and scalar multiples, but reversing
the input order changes the sign.
Area uses the magnitude, so it is nonnegative regardless of that orientation
sign.
A supporting application combines the two vector products into a scalar triple
product.
Write u dot the quantity v cross w.
Its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped with edge vectors u, v
and w.
The sign records orientation, while geometric volume is nonnegative.
With mutually perpendicular edges two, zero, zero; zero, three, zero; and
zero,
zero, four, the triple product is twenty four.
The volume is twenty four cubic units, and the tetrahedron formed by those
three edges from one vertex has one sixth of that volume, or four.
A cyclic permutation of the three vectors preserves the triple product, while
swapping two reverses its sign.
A zero triple product means the three vectors are linearly dependent and lie
in
a common plane through their shared tail, including degenerate zero cases.
To test four points for coplanarity, form three displacement vectors from one
selected point rather than using three unrelated position vectors.
These volume and coplanarity examples support the main scalar and vector
product methods and the preceding 3D Geometry class.
Retain brackets so the cross product is calculated before the final dot
product.
A mixed vector question is easier when the required geometric condition
determines the operation.
Equality uses corresponding components.
A magnitude uses the square root of a self dot product.
Perpendicular nonzero vectors have dot product zero, while parallel nonzero
vectors have proportional components or zero cross product.
An area uses a cross product magnitude.
For u equal to one, two, negative one and v equal to two, k, four,
perpendicularity gives two plus two k minus four equal to zero, so k equals
one.
Substituting that value restores a zero dot product and both vectors remain
nonzero.
Do not solve a dot product equation for a parameter and forget to check a
condition that excludes the zero vector.
Similarly, cancelling a possibly zero component in a proportionality equation
can remove valid cases.
Keep track of the type of each result: a sum and a cross product are vectors,
whereas a magnitude and a dot product are scalars.
A diagram can suggest a direction or sign, but component verification
establishes the numerical answer.
Final checks should include the original condition, any normalization
denominator and the units of a geometric length, area or volume.
